c.tagline: Cobblestone old town, golden Pacific beaches, and Mexico's most welcoming beach city on the Bay of Banderas.

taxi.fareNote: Puerto Vallarta taxis are not metered — agree the fare before getting in, as drivers charge by zone. Uber and DiDi both operate and are usually cheaper, though taxi unions restrict app pickups at some spots like the airport and Marina.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line, and Puerto Vallarta has a dedicated tourist police force.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.El Centro (Malecón): Malecon Puerto Vallarta Our Lady of Guadalupe

avoid.reason: Tourist zone safe; caution downtown at night; avoid drug involvement (cartel presence)

hood_desc: The lively heart of Puerto Vallarta's tourism south of the Cuale River, centered on Los Muertos Beach, the Basilio Badillo 'Restaurant Row,' and Olas Altas; it's the walkable hub of the city's dining, bars, and famously vibrant LGBTQ+ nightlife.

The historic downtown north of the river along the oceanfront Malecón boardwalk, home to the Church of Our Lady of Guadalupe, sculpture-lined promenades, art galleries, and the main plaza; best for first-timers who want sights, street life, and cobblestone charm.

A planned upscale resort district around a yacht-filled marina north of downtown, with a golf course, waterfront restaurants, condos, and big-brand hotels; suits travelers wanting a calm, self-contained base near the airport.

The strip of large beachfront resort hotels lining the bay between downtown and the Marina; a convenient, low-key all-inclusive base with easy beach access, though it lacks the character of the old town.

An exclusive hillside neighborhood just south of the Romantic Zone with dramatic bay views, secluded rocky coves, and luxury villas and boutique hotels; suits couples and travelers wanting a quiet, scenic, upscale retreat.

water.note: The city certifies its municipal supply, but nearly everyone drinks bottled or purified water.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:00am to 11:00pm along the main Highway 200 corridor; water taxis run in daylight hours. Late-night travel relies on taxis or ride apps.
transit.note: There is no metro, tram, or rail; getting around means cheap urban buses along the bay, taxis, ride-hail apps, or water taxis from the Los Muertos and Boca de Tomatlán piers to the roadless southern-shore beaches.
transit.pay: City buses ('camiones') are paid in cash to the driver, about MXN 10-12 (~US$0.60) per ride; there is no rechargeable transit card. Buses are marked by destination (Centro, Marina, Tunel, Aeropuerto) and run the main corridors. Water taxis to southern beaches like Yelapa and Las Ánimas are paid in cash at the pier.

food.name: Birria tacos
food.desc: Jalisco's slow-stewed beef or goat, spooned into tortillas dipped in the red fat and served with a cup of consome for dunking.

places.name: Birria Chanfay
places.note: Street cart running since 1972 on Venustiano Carranza; the city's most famous birria stand.

places.name: El Camaron Express
places.note: Handmade corn tortillas, barbacoa-style birria and rich consome; widely rated the best in town.

places.name: Mercado Municipal Rio Cuale
places.note: Upstairs market fondas serve birria and other Jalisco stews at local prices.

food.name: Tacos de camaron
food.desc: Pacific shrimp battered and fried or grilled with garlic, tucked into tortillas with cabbage, crema and a squeeze of lime.

places.name: El Camaron Express
places.note: Shrimp is the whole point here; large menu, quick service, closed Sundays.

places.name: Marisma Fish Taco
places.note: Cash-only taco truck with a permanent queue, famous for battered shrimp and fish tacos.

places.name: It's Taco Time
places.note: Small cart off the boardwalk where shrimp and marlin tacos are the customer favourites.

food.name: Pescado zarandeado
food.desc: A whole butterflied snapper rubbed with chile and mayonnaise-mustard adobo, clamped in a grill basket and smoked over charcoal for the table to share.

places.name: Mariscos Tino's
places.note: Twenty-plus years of practice; zarandeado is the house specialty and a local institution.

places.name: Ramada El Chavo
places.note: Pick and weigh your snapper, then wait 45 minutes for it to come off the charcoal.

places.name: Boca de Tomatlan palapas
places.note: Fishing-village beach palapas grilling the morning's catch; the most scenic version.

food.name: Tacos al pastor
food.desc: Adobo-marinated pork carved off the spit with a slice of pineapple. In Vallarta it is a late-night ritual after the Malecon.

places.name: Pancho's Takos
places.note: Vallarta's best-known pastor spot; expect a line down Basilio Badillo after dark.

places.name: Tacos Robles
places.note: Neighbourhood trompo in a residential barrio where locals outnumber visitors.

places.name: Mercado Municipal Rio Cuale
places.note: Cheap, quick pastor tacos among the market's food counters by the river.

food.name: Tacos de marlin
food.desc: Smoked marlin shredded and sauteed with tomato and chile, then wrapped in a flour tortilla or burrito. A Nayarit-Jalisco coastal staple.

places.name: Tacon de Marlin
places.note: Legendary first-and-last stop for smoked marlin burritos; open early and constantly busy.

places.name: It's Taco Time
places.note: Melt-in-the-mouth marlin is the cart's signature, served with punchy house sauces.

places.name: Marisma Fish Taco
places.note: Seafood taco truck where marlin sits alongside the famous shrimp and fish versions.

food.name: Raicilla
food.desc: Jalisco's coastal agave spirit, distilled in the Sierra above Vallarta and once smuggled in by boat. Earthier and more herbal than tequila.

places.name: El Tasting Room
places.note: Downtown bar built around raicilla with scheduled formal tastings of agave spirits.

places.name: Chiro
places.note: Named for the raicilla smuggling boats; coastal raicilla, cheap beer and DJ nights.

places.name: Savia Agave Niche
places.note: Woman-owned agave bar with a curated raicilla, mezcal and tequila list; closed Mondays.

food.name: Agua de horchata
food.desc: Iced rice-and-cinnamon water, poured from big glass vitroleros beside jamaica and tamarindo. The default soft drink with tacos and seafood.

places.name: Mercado Municipal Rio Cuale
places.note: Market juice counters blend aguas frescas fresh each morning at local prices.

places.name: Pancho's Takos
places.note: Horchata and jamaica by the jug to cut the heat of the pastor tacos.

places.name: Mariscos Tino's
places.note: Family seafood house where aguas frescas come by the pitcher for the table.

landmarks: El Malecón
A mile-long oceanfront esplanade strung with whimsical bronze sculptures, street performers and sunset views that define the soul of Puerto Vallarta.
Parroquia de Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe
The city's beloved crown-topped church rising above the old town, its wrought-iron corona the most recognisable silhouette on the skyline.
Zona Romántica
Cobblestoned streets of galleries, taco stands and lively bars south of the Río Cuale, the city's most charming and walkable neighbourhood.
Playa Los Muertos and Pier
Vallarta's busiest beach, anchored by a futuristic sail-shaped pier that glows at night and launches water taxis to hidden coves.
Los Arcos Marine Park
Granite arches rising from the sea off Mismaloya, a protected snorkelling and diving reserve teeming with parrotfish, rays and sea turtles.
Islas Marietas
A day-trip archipelago and national park famed for its hidden Playa del Amor, a beach concealed inside a collapsed volcanic crater.
Isla Cuale
A leafy river island in the city centre, threaded with craft markets, iguanas and footbridges linking downtown to the Romantic Zone.
Vallarta Botanical Garden
Mountain gardens south of town showcasing Mexico's orchids, agaves and vanilla vines, with river swimming and abundant hummingbirds among the jungle.
Mirador de La Cruz
A steep climb from downtown to a hilltop cross rewarding hikers with the definitive panorama of red-tiled roofs and Banderas Bay.
Boca de Tomatlán
A fishing village where the jungle meets the sea, gateway to water taxis and coastal trails toward the beach hamlets of Colomitos and Yelapa.

train.note: No passenger railway reaches Puerto Vallarta - Mexico's rail network is freight-only on this coast. Arrive by coach along Highway 200, or fly into the international airport just north of town, which is the way most visitors come.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Central Camionera is about 10 km north near the airport, with ETN (https://www.etn.com.mx/) and Primera Plus (https://www.primeraplus.com.mx/) running to Guadalajara in about 5 hours, Mexico City overnight and Mazatlán up the coast. Local buses along the coast road reach Sayulita, Bucerías and the southern beaches.

intl.to: Yelapa, Quimixto & Las Ánimas (Mexico) - south-shore beaches with no road access
intl.op: water-taxi operators from Los Muertos pier and Boca de Tomatlán — tickets at the pier

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international or long-distance ferry from Puerto Vallarta. The water taxis matter here because several villages along the southern shore of Banderas Bay have no road at all - the boat is the only way in. They run to a rough timetable from the Los Muertos pier and more frequently from Boca de Tomatlán, and the last return of the day is early, so check it before you go.

half.name: Sayulita
half.blurb: Surf town in Nayarit about 45 km north has a laid-back beach break, jungle-backed hills and a compact grid of colorful streets.

half.name: Punta Mita
half.blurb: Peninsula resort area about 45 km north sits at the tip of Banderas Bay, with reef breaks and calm coves.

half.name: Yelapa
half.blurb: Secluded beach village reached by boat across the bay has no road access and a waterfall a short walk from the shore.

half.name: San Sebastián del Oeste
half.blurb: Colonial silver-mining town in the Sierra Madre, about 80 km east, preserves cobblestone streets and raicilla distilleries.

half.name: Bucerías
half.blurb: Beach town about 25 km north has a long uninterrupted stretch of sand and a Thursday street market known for artisan crafts.
